title: A workflow redesign
scenario: You are head of customer operations at an energy supplier with 600 staff. The billing-complaints desk has 25 people and answers about 1,200 emails a week. Management wants an AI-supported redesign of the desk's workflow, and you must propose it. The exhibit holds the draft and what you know. All numbers are made up for this case.
exhibit:
BRIEF:
  Most emails are about a wrong bill.
  Goal: faster replies, without more wrong credits.
  The firm uses a ChatGPT Enterprise workspace.

DRAFT WORKFLOW:
  1  Read the email and sort it: wrong bill, meter reading, payment plan
  2  Look up the account history in the billing system
     (the same lookup, in the same order, every time)
  3  Draft the reply
  4  Apply a bill credit (money leaves the company)
  5  Send the reply

TEAM IDEA (from the team lead):
  Five agents work on each reply: history, tone, credit amount, legal wording
  and summary. All five need the same account history, and each one uses the
  work of the one before it.

ACCESS NOTE:
  The quality manager wants to see how much the desk uses the assistant.
  She must not be able to change any setting.

SETUP TEST SO FAR:
  The IT administrator signed in, asked the assistant to look up an account,
  and it worked. Next step planned: open it to all 25 desk agents.

FIRST PILOT TEAM (6 agents, before launch and 3 months after):
                                     Before    After
  Messages per agent per week          40        72
  Days to resolve a complaint          4.2       4.1
  Repeat complaints within 30 days     8%        11%
  The VP says: "Usage is up 80%, so the redesign works."

questions.prompt: Which is the best view of the team lead's five-agent idea for one reply?

options.text: A good idea, because more agents always finish faster and the cost rises only a little with each one.
options.explanation: Each extra agent adds token cost. Anthropic's research post reports about 15 times more tokens for multi-agent systems than for chat.

options.text: A poor fit: all five need the same history and depend on each other, so one agent should write the reply.
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic's post says work where all agents share the same context, or depend on each other a lot, is not a good fit for multi-agent systems.

options.text: A good fit, because each agent has a different skill, and different skills should be split between agents.
options.explanation: Skills alone are not the test. The parts must be fairly independent, and these five each use the work of the one before.

options.text: A good fit if all five run at the same time, because work done in parallel always finishes sooner.
options.explanation: Each agent needs the previous agent's work, so they cannot run side by side. Waiting and handing over work add cost.

questions.prompt: Step 2 uses the same lookup, in the same order, every time. How should it be built?

options.text: As an agent that picks its own tools and its own order each time, because that is the most flexible choice for the desk.
options.explanation: Anthropic's post says agents suit work that needs flexibility. A lookup that never changes does not need it.

options.text: As a manager agent that invents new helper agents for every email, because each email is different and the plan can adapt.
options.explanation: The lookup is the same each time, so there is nothing new to plan. Extra helper agents add cost and add no value here.

options.text: As a loop where one model call writes the lookup and another grades it, so that mistakes are caught before the result is used.
options.explanation: A loop with a grader fits work with clear criteria that needs revising. A fixed lookup has no draft to improve.

options.text: As a fixed step on a set path: code runs the same lookup every time, and the model works only on the wording of the reply.
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic's post says workflows, with predefined code paths, offer predictability and consistency for well-defined tasks.

questions.prompt: Which built-in role fits the quality manager's access in OpenAI's ChatGPT Enterprise guide?

options.text: The Analytics Viewer role, which the guide lists as the built-in role that can open workspace analytics.
options.explanation: Right. OpenAI's roles guide lists Analytics Viewer as the built-in role that can access workspace analytics. Its rollout guide says to keep administration roles for people who administer.

options.text: The Admin role, because anyone who looks at workspace data should be able to manage the workspace as well.
options.explanation: Admin manages supported operations and groups. She would get power she does not need, and the guide says to keep it limited.

options.text: The Owner role, because the Owner is the only person who is allowed to open the workspace analytics.
options.explanation: The guide names Analytics Viewer for analytics. Owner manages workspace-wide settings, which is more power than she needs.

options.text: A custom role, because custom roles are the way to set how much administrative power a member holds.
options.explanation: Custom roles define which supported features a member can use. Built-in roles set administrative authority.

questions.prompt: The setup worked for the IT administrator. What should the rollout add before it opens to all 25 agents?

options.text: Nothing more: a setup that works for an administrator will work in the same way for every employee.
options.explanation: An administrator's account has more rights than an agent's. A setup can pass for IT and still fail for an ordinary employee.

options.text: A second test by the same administrator, on another day, to be sure that the first result still holds.
options.explanation: The same account would show the same result. The gap is the account, not the day of the test.

options.text: A test with a representative agent: an ordinary member who holds the permissions that agents will have.
options.explanation: Right. OpenAI's rollout guide says to verify each boundary with representative identities. Find the problem in the test, not on the first morning.

options.text: A written note from the vendor that the setup is correct, filed with the plan before the rollout starts.
options.explanation: A vendor note does not show how your own roles and permissions behave for your own agents. Only a test with a real member does.

questions.prompt: The VP says usage is up 80%, so the redesign works. What does the pilot team's data show?

options.text: It works: more messages means more finished work, and the pilot is a good sign for the whole desk.
options.explanation: OpenAI's Usage Insights page says a message count does not tell you how much work the team finished.

options.text: Not proven yet: messages measure use only, while resolve time barely moved and repeat complaints rose.
options.explanation: Right. OpenAI's page says to pair usage with team records to see whether work takes less effort or meets quality standards. Here quality looks worse.

options.text: It fails: repeat complaints rose from 8% to 11%, so the desk should stop using the assistant right now.
options.explanation: One pilot of 6 agents is too small to prove failure. It is a reason to look at why repeat complaints rose, then test again.

options.text: It works for speed: days to resolve fell, so the rise in repeat complaints can be left out of the report.
options.explanation: The fall is only 0.1 of a day. A guard number that gets worse should be shown, not left out.
